title: The Long Road | A Night at the Greek Theatre
subtitle: A record of a moment of happiness.
body:
At the Greek Theatre under the night sky, the cello was imitating a horse’s neigh. The sound seemed to come from far away, free and clear, carrying something of a primal cry. It brought to mind the pilot in *West with the Night*—crossing the African night sky alone, entrusting her fate to the wind and stars; or the coffee farmer in *Out of Africa*—leaving Europe to embrace the land and culture of another place. Their choices held loneliness and hardship, but also vastness and freedom. A voice sounded in my mind: “Freedom is not a future reward, but the breath we take in the present.”

The atmosphere of Berkeley echoed this feeling. Here, the heavy melodies of Mahler and Tchaikovsky share a stage with African drumbeats; classical Chinese dance shares a space with avant-garde theatre. Cultures meet here as equals, without obscuring one another. It is hard for children growing up in such an atmosphere to become narrow nationalists. What they absorb is vastness, and also gentleness.

The music continued to flow. A melody in Yo-Yo Ma’s solo—perhaps *Jasmine Flower*—grew from the depths of the cello, like a dark river passing through the night sky, suddenly and quietly connecting me to my homeland. In that moment, I remembered a sentence from an old book: *“On mornings in a foreign country, I often wake alone and hear birds singing outside the window, yet feel that I can no longer understand the language they speak.”* That loneliness, I too had tasted during the pandemic years.

On those nights, I dreamed of home again and again. The streets and the shadows of trees in my dreams were so clear that I seemed able to reach out and touch them, yet a thin mist I could not cross always lay between us. And so, even in my dreams, I came to a clear realization: home had become a distant place I could no longer reach. But fate had not denied me opportunities: the summer after the exams, the winter night when the pandemic first began, that midsummer when quarantine restrictions eased. Hailuo’s voice kept echoing in my ears: “Wait a little longer. It won’t be too late to come back next year. Your degree matters more.” Yet looking back, those reasons were all like scraps of paper scattered by the wind, turning in the air, falling, without a sound.

The music also reminded us of the weight of the world. Before Kidjo began singing *Aisha*, Yo-Yo Ma said softly, “Children don’t cry.” A simple sentence, yet like a key, it unlocked pain beyond words. Stifled sobs came from the darkness; I knew I was not the only one struck by it. The music pointed to nothing in particular, yet left a blank space for everyone, allowing each person’s wounds to surface—the firelight still burning among the ruins, the long wait beside an empty bowl, the tears held back in a child’s eyes, and the hatred burning in vain within the chest.

In that heavy echo, I understood more clearly how I wanted to live: not as the Master trapped in the Glass Bead Game, confining a lifetime within an isolated purity; nor spending all my energy on achievements and empty renown, but, like a certain someone, simply “loafing” and following my own path.[1] Closer to what I wanted was to feel my way along the river, leaving again and again through its rises and falls, and returning again and again, until I found some balance between the earthly world and the soul—
to be able to weep in music, to find release in the laughter of friends, to listen to the great wind howl.

I still admire those who are utterly pure. Tarkovsky, for instance, who burned through his life in devotion. But that is not my path. My devotion is closer to an ordinary yet steadfast stance: *enjoy every moment, and never regret.*

The lingering notes of the cello still echoed in the air. That neighing sound was like the cry beneath the night sky at the beginning, yet it was no longer merely an echo from afar. It reminded me: freedom is not a future reward, but the breath we take in the present; happiness is not a bargaining chip for sacrifice, but the clear flow of life in this very moment.

And so the music of this night was like a musical movement: vast in its opening, heavy in its depths, yet coming to rest in peace at its close. It let me know how I would go on.

---

[1] “Loafing” alludes to Larry in W. Somerset Maugham’s *The Razor’s Edge*, whose choice to step outside a conventional career allows him to pursue questions about life and its meaning.
